notes: Ruling slot 23 = House of Khalifa (Isa bin Salman). MD's duplicate Al Khalifa entry in slot 0 replaced by the British-led Special Branch (Ian Henderson). Slot 13 switches from the Administrative Council to the Council of State on 19 Jan 1970 (decreed administrative reform, not a regime change). Ba'ath kept in slot 21 as in MD; Nasserists fill slot 7. Shia slots: Akhbari traditionalists 6, Dawa 8, Shirazi Risaliyyun 9, Ja'fari Endowments 14. Al-Islah Society (MB) in 12 as precursor of MD's Al-Menbar; NLF in 4 as precursor of MD's Progressive Democratic Tribune.

0.name: Bahrain Special Branch
0.text:
The Special Branch is the political police of Bahrain's British-officered police force, charged with watching the underground left, the Arab nationalist clubs and the Shia seminarians returning from Iraq. Since 1966 it has been run by Ian Henderson, a veteran of the Mau Mau emergency in Kenya, who works closely with the British Political Residency in Bahrain.

Its creed is order before politics: informers in the suq and the refinery, detention without trial and the deportation of troublesome expatriates. It regards a continued British or American presence after 1971 as the best guarantee of stability. Its leverage lies in its files, its loyalty to the Ruler and its say over who is arrested, exiled or pardoned.

1.name: Majlis Baladiyyat al-Manama
1.text:
Founded in 1919 as the first municipality in the Gulf, the Manama Municipal Council brings together merchants, landlords and community notables to run the capital's markets, roads, water supply and building permits. It works under the Ruler's authority and within the limits set by the Al Khalifa and their British advisers.

Its members favour gradual reform: a consultative role for notables, sound budgets, modern services and an orderly end to the protectorate that keeps close ties with Britain and the West. Revolution and sectarian politics alarm them. Their leverage lies in the trust of the commercial classes and in presiding over the oldest representative body Bahrain has known.

2.name: Nadi al-'Uruba
2.text:
The Uruba (Arabism) Club was founded in Manama in 1939 by young educated Bahrainis and has ever since been a meeting place for teachers, clerks, lawyers and merchants' sons who debate politics under the cover of literary evenings and lectures. Veterans of the reform movement of the 1950s still gather there, watched closely by the Special Branch.

Its members want a written constitution, an elected assembly, a free press and modern Arabic education, and they insist that Bahrain is an Arab country whatever Tehran claims. They reject sectarianism and favour cooperation with the other Gulf emirates. Their influence is moral rather than organised: they shape opinion among the educated middle class and supply the petitions and newspaper columns of Bahraini reformism.

3.name: Lijan 'Ummal BAPCO
3.text:
The Bahrain Petroleum Company's refinery at Sitra and its oilfield around Awali employ thousands of Bahrainis, Shia villagers and Sunni townsmen side by side. Since the company's redundancies sparked the March uprising of 1965, informal workers' committees have kept alive the demand for a legal trade union, which neither the company nor the Ruler permits.

The committees want a labour law with the right to organise, collective bargaining, Bahrainisation of skilled posts, pensions and protection against mass layoffs. They prefer negotiation and strikes to underground politics, and many would accept a British-style system of industrial relations rather than revolution. Their leverage is the refinery itself: a stoppage at Sitra strikes at the state's main source of revenue and employment.

4.name: Jabhat al-Tahrir al-Watani – al-Bahrayn
4.text:
Founded in 1955, the National Liberation Front is Bahrain's communist party and the oldest Marxist organisation in the Gulf. Banned and hunted by the Special Branch, it works through clandestine cells among refinery workers, teachers and students, while many of its cadres live in exile in Baghdad, Damascus, Beirut and the socialist countries after the arrests that followed the 1965 uprising.

It follows the Soviet line: an end to British bases and the treaties, a democratic constitution, legal trade unions, nationalisation of oil and friendship with the USSR. It recruits across the sectarian divide, emphasising class over sect. Its leverage lies in its disciplined underground, its influence in workplace committees and its links with Moscow and the Iraqi communists.

5.name: Al-Jabha al-Sha'biyya li-Tahrir al-Khalij al-'Arabi al-Muhtall
5.english: Popular Front for the Liberation of the Occupied Arab Gulf
5.native_full: Al-Jabha al-Sha'biyya li-Tahrir al-Khalij al-'Arabi al-Muhtall
5.text:
The Popular Front for the Liberation of the Occupied Arab Gulf grew out of the Dhofar insurgency, and at its Hamrin congress in 1968 it adopted Marxism-Leninism and extended its struggle to the whole Gulf. In Bahrain its supporters are former Arab Nationalist Movement cadres of the 1965 uprising, organised from exile by Abdulrahman al-Nuaimi.

The Front rejects both the federation of shaikhs and the British withdrawal settlement as a new colonial arrangement, and calls for people's war against the Al Khalifa, the oil companies and the British bases. It looks to China and South Yemen for arms and training. In Bahrain its strength lies in student and youth networks, clandestine printing and the prestige of the Dhofar guerrillas.
5.wiki: Popular Front for the Liberation of Oman

6.name: Al-Akhbariyyun
6.text:
Bahrain is the historic heartland of the Akhbari school of Shia jurisprudence, which rejects the independent reasoning of the Usuli mujtahids and holds to the literal reports of the Imams. Its shaikhs lead prayers, ma'tams and village arbitration across the Shia countryside, and they look with suspicion on the young Najaf graduates now returning home with political ideas.

The Akhbaris are deeply hostile to Western schooling, cinemas, alcohol and the moral influence of the British base and the oil company, and would rather see religious life ruled by custom than by any party. They shun nationalism and communism alike. Their leverage is the loyalty of older Baharna villagers and their role in marriages, inheritances and endowments in dozens of villages.

7.name: Al-Nasiriyyun
7.text:
Since the Suez crisis of 1956, when crowds in Manama attacked British property, Gamal Abdel Nasser has been the hero of Bahrain's Arab nationalist street. The Nasserists are a loose following of teachers, clerks, students and Egyptian-trained graduates who listen to Sawt al-Arab from Cairo, without a legal organisation since the reform movement was crushed in 1956.

They want the British gone, Bahrain's Arab identity affirmed against the Iranian claim and the country drawn into Cairo's camp under a strong, modernising leadership on the Egyptian pattern. Their model is a single-party, army-backed Arab socialist state rather than parliamentary pluralism. Their leverage is emotional: in a crisis, Cairo's word can still bring the youth of Manama and Muharraq into the streets.

8.name: Hizb al-Da'wa al-Islamiyya
8.text:
The Islamic Dawa Party was founded in Najaf in the late 1950s by Shia clerics around Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr to answer communism and secular nationalism with an Islamic political programme. Bahraini seminarians studying in Najaf have carried its ideas and cell structure home, where it works discreetly through mosques, ma'tams and religious study circles.

It seeks an Islamic society built through education and gradual mobilisation rather than violent revolt, and is prepared to contest elections should Bahrain ever obtain a parliament. It opposes Western cultural influence and Soviet atheism alike, and wants Shia citizens to have a fair share of jobs and public life. Its strength lies among young educated Shia and the rising generation of reformist clerics.

9.name: Al-Risaliyyun
9.text:
The Risaliyyun are the activist wing of the school of Grand Ayatollah Muhammad al-Shirazi in Karbala, organised by his nephews Muhammad Taqi al-Modarresi and Hadi al-Modarresi. Their clandestine network reaches into the Gulf through Bahraini students in the Karbala seminaries and through the pilgrims and merchants who travel between Iraq and Manama.

They preach that the clergy must lead the community and that a righteous Islamic order will be won by a disciplined revolutionary vanguard, not by notables or parties. They reject the Al Khalifa, the British and the Shah's claim alike. Their leverage is the fervour of young converts and a readiness for confrontation that the cautious village clergy lack.

10.name: Idarat al-Awqaf al-Sunniyya
10.text:
The Sunni Endowments Directorate administers the mosques, religious trusts and Quranic schools of Bahrain's Sunni community and works alongside the Sunni Shari'a courts, whose qadis are appointed by the Ruler. Its 'ulama, mostly of the Maliki and Shafi'i schools, preach in the mosques of Muharraq, Riffa and Manama and owe their positions to the Al Khalifa.

They teach obedience to the legitimate ruler, defend Shari'a in family law and look to Saudi Arabia as guardian of the holy places and natural ally of the dynasty. They distrust both the Muslim Brotherhood's activism and the secular nationalists. Their leverage lies in the pulpit, the courts and the religious legitimacy they lend to the ruling family.

11.name: Hizb al-Tahrir
11.text:
Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Party of Liberation founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by Taqi al-Din al-Nabhani, works across the Arab world through secret study circles that aim to restore the caliphate. In Bahrain its small cells recruit among Jordanian and Palestinian teachers and a few Sunni students, and its leaflets circulate quietly in Manama's schools and mosques.

The party rejects nation-states, monarchies, parliaments and nationalism as un-Islamic, and condemns the American and Soviet blocs alike. It seeks to win over influential men, above all officers, so that power can be seized and handed to a single caliph ruling by Shari'a. Its strength is ideological discipline rather than numbers.

12.name: Jam'iyyat al-Islah
12.text:
The Al-Islah (Reform) Society began in 1941 as a students' club in Muharraq and took its present name in 1948, becoming the home of the Muslim Brotherhood's ideas among Bahrain's Sunnis. It is a legal association, and its president, Shaikh Isa bin Muhammad Al Khalifa, is a member of the ruling family.

Its programme is religious and social: Islamic education, charity, sports and lectures that shape a pious, modern-educated Sunni middle class. It opposes communism and secular nationalism, distrusts Shia activism and prefers the conservative Arab monarchies to Cairo's revolution. Its leverage lies in its respectability, its schools and youth activities and its access to the palace through its royal president.

13.name: Al-Majlis al-Idari
13.text:
The Administrative Council is the executive arm of the Ruler's government, bringing together the heads of the departments of finance, police, education, health, public works and the municipalities. It is presided over by Shaikh Khalifa bin Salman Al Khalifa, the Ruler's younger brother and the dominant figure in Bahrain's administration.

Its outlook is that of a modernising bureaucracy: planned development, diversification away from dwindling oil through industry such as the planned aluminium smelter, a well-paid civil service and the gradual replacement of British advisers by Bahraini officials. It prefers administration to politics and sees no hurry for elections. Its power rests on the budget, appointments and the machinery that will become the government of an independent state.

13.name: Majlis al-Dawla
13.text:
Created by decree of the Ruler in January 1970, the Council of State replaces the old Administrative Council as Bahrain's cabinet in all but name. Its departmental directors act as ministers, and it is presided over by Shaikh Khalifa bin Salman Al Khalifa, the Ruler's brother and the real manager of government.

It stands for planned development, industrial diversification, a Bahraini civil service in place of British advisers and careful preparation for full independence. It treats political participation as something to be granted from above and in measured doses. Its power rests on the budget, appointments and the state machinery that an independent Bahrain will inherit.

14.name: Idarat al-Awqaf al-Ja'fariyya
14.text:
The Ja'fari Endowments Directorate manages the mosques, ma'tams and religious trusts of Bahrain's Shia majority, and together with the Ja'fari courts it is the main channel between the Baharna villages and the state. Its council is drawn from established clerical and merchant families who have learned to work with the Al Khalifa since the reforms of the 1920s.

The notables around it seek fair treatment for the Shia, protection of their religious institutions and a share of jobs and services, but they shun underground parties and Iranian or Iraqi adventures. They prefer petitions to protests and negotiation to confrontation. Their leverage is communal: they speak for the Shia countryside and can calm it or let it boil.

15.name: Ghurfat Tijarat wa-Sina'at al-Bahrayn
15.english: Bahrain Chamber of Commerce and Industry
15.text:
Founded in 1939, the Bahrain Chamber of Commerce and Industry is the voice of the island's great merchant houses, among them the Kanoo, Almoayyed, Fakhro and Zayani families, whose shipping, trading and agency businesses tie Bahrain to British, American and Indian commerce. Its leading members are consulted by the Ruler on economic policy.

The Chamber wants stability above all: a smooth transition to independence, continued British and American business, commercial agencies reserved for Bahraini nationals and a future as the Gulf's centre for services and banking as oil declines. It fears both revolution and absorption by Iran. Its leverage lies in money, credit and long-standing personal ties to the ruling family.

16.name: Tujjar al-Suq
16.text:
The shopkeepers, gold dealers, money changers, wholesalers and dhow traders of the Manama and Muharraq bazaars form a world of their own, Arab, Persian and Indian, that lives from the island's role as an entrepot for the Gulf. They have no organisation beyond guild custom and their evening majlises, but there they talk politics every night.

They want low customs duties, a free port, few licences, a sound Bahraini dinar and as little state interference as possible. They distrust both the planners of the Administrative Council and the socialists of the underground. Their leverage lies in their numbers, their capital and their role as the daily link between Bahrain and its neighbours.

17.name: Ahl al-Bahr
17.text:
The People of the Sea are the fishermen, former pearl divers, boat-builders and fish-trap owners of Bahrain's coastal villages, from Sitra and Nabih Saleh to Hidd. Pearling collapsed a generation ago, and now they watch the refinery, land reclamation and new jetties eat into the reefs, mangroves and fishing grounds their families have worked for centuries.

They ask for protection of the pearl banks and fish stocks, limits on oil discharges and reclamation, and care for the island's freshwater springs, which are running dry as new wells draw down the aquifer. They have little organisation and speak through elders and clerics. Their leverage is moral and local: they embody a heritage every Bahraini claims as his own.

18.name: Usrat al-Udaba' wa-l-Kuttab
18.text:
Founded in 1969 by a new generation of poets, critics and storytellers, the Writers Association has quickly become the most outspoken civic platform in Bahrain. Among its founders is the young poet Qassim Haddad, and its readings, journals and debates draw students, teachers and workers into discussion of literature and politics alike.

Its members stand for modern Arabic culture, freedom of expression, social justice and an Arab, non-aligned Bahrain free of foreign bases. They sympathise with Arab socialism and with the anti-imperialist movements from Vietnam to Palestine, without binding themselves to any party line. Their leverage is cultural: they shape the language and imagination of the educated young and lend prestige to the opposition.

19.name: Jil al-Intifada
19.text:
The Intifada Generation are the students and young workers radicalised by the March uprising of 1965, when schoolboys and refinery hands fought the police for weeks in Muharraq, Manama and Sitra. Now studying in Cairo, Baghdad, Kuwait and Beirut or back in Bahrain's secondary schools, they read Mao, Guevara and Fanon and owe allegiance to no established party.

They scorn the National Liberation Front's Moscow line as timid and the old nationalists as compromised, and call for a people's war on the Chinese and Vietnamese model that would sweep away the shaikhs and the British together. They are few, young and divided, but their pamphlets and wall slogans are spreading, and they supply recruits to whoever offers action.

20.name: Al-Bahrayn 'Arabiyya
20.text:
Bahrain Is Arab is the rallying cry of the townsmen who answer Iran's claim to the islands with petitions, sermons, club rallies and wall slogans. It is strongest in the popular quarters of Muharraq and among the sports and cultural clubs, and it grows louder as Britain and Iran search for a formula to settle the claim before the British leave.

Its populism mixes pride in Arab identity with resentment of the Persian merchants, Indian clerks and Pakistani labourers who seem to hold the island's jobs and shops. It demands jobs for Bahrainis first, curbs on immigration and Arabic in public life. Its leverage is numbers in the streets at a moment when Bahrain's very identity is in question.

21.name: Hizb al-Ba'th al-'Arabi al-Ishtiraki
21.text:
Ba'athist cells have existed in Bahrain since the 1950s, recruited among teachers, students and civil servants who studied in Baghdad, Damascus and Beirut. Since the party's split in 1966 most Bahraini Ba'athists look to the Iraqi leadership that took power in Baghdad in July 1968 under Ahmed Hassan al-Bakr, and they operate clandestinely under the eye of the Special Branch.

The party preaches unity, freedom and socialism: one Arab nation from the Atlantic to the Gulf, an end to British bases and the shaikhly order, and rule by a disciplined vanguard party. It is fiercely hostile to Iran's claim and to its communist rivals. Its leverage lies in Iraqi money, scholarships and propaganda, and in its appeal to Arab nationalists.

22.name: Quwwat Difa' al-Bahrayn
22.text:
The Bahrain Defence Force was founded on 5 February 1968 as the island's first national army, under the command of the Crown Prince, Shaikh Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa, a graduate of Mons Officer Cadet School. Small, lightly armed and still trained by British officers, it is preparing to take over the defence of the island when British forces leave.

Its officer corps is drawn largely from the ruling family and loyal Sunni tribes, and it sees itself as guardian of the dynasty, of Bahrain's Arab identity against Iran and of order against subversion. It has no political programme beyond loyalty to the Ruler. Its leverage lies in being the only armed force under exclusively Bahraini command.

23.name: Al Khalifa
23.text:
The Al Khalifa have ruled Bahrain since they conquered the islands from Zubara in 1783. The Ruler, Shaikh Isa bin Salman Al Khalifa, has reigned since 1961; his brother Khalifa bin Salman runs the administration and his son Hamad commands the new defence force. Britain conducts the state's foreign relations and defence under treaties it has announced will end in 1971.

The family governs through the Ruler's majlis, land grants, tribal alliances and a British-built administration, and intends to keep all real authority while offering limited consultation. Its priorities are ending Iran's claim, securing a place in a Gulf federation or going alone, and keeping Western protection in another form. Its leverage is legitimacy, land, revenue and the loyalty of the army and police.
